title: Kare-Kare
description: Oxtail simmered for hours until fall-apart tender, then folded into a thick roasted-peanut sauce with eggplant and long beans — a festive stew served with a side of shrimp paste for kick.

ingredients.note: or 3 tbsp regular rice flour toasted dry in a pan until light gold
or substitute a second eggplant if unavailable

ingredients.item: Chinese eggplant, sliced into thick rounds

steps: Rinse the oxtail and place in a large pot with the water; bring to a boil over medium heat, skimming off the scum that rises.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer 2.5-3 hours until the oxtail is easily pierced with a fork, topping up water as needed; strain and reserve the broth, keeping the meat separate.
Blanch the eggplant, long beans and banana blossom in salted boiling water for 1-2 minutes each until just tender-crisp; set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pot and sauté the onion and garlic until softened; add the oxtail and cook, stirring, until lightly browned.
Pour in the fish sauce, then add about 6 cups of the reserved broth and bring to a boil.
Whisk the toasted rice flour with a little water into a smooth slurry, then stir it into the pot to thicken the broth slightly.
Stir in the peanut butter until fully dissolved and the sauce turns thick and creamy; season with salt and pepper.
Add the blanched vegetables and bok choy, folding gently until coated and heated through, then serve hot with rice and sautéed bagoong on the side.
tips: Toasting the rice flour dry in a pan first adds a nutty background note that plain flour doesn't.
The peanut sauce should coat a spoon thickly but still pour — thin it with a splash of reserved broth if it seizes up.
Oxtail is easiest to portion after it's chilled slightly; ask the butcher to pre-cut it if your knife struggles.
nutritionNote: Rich in fat from both the oxtail and peanut sauce, so serve modest portions of sauce over a normal rice serving and lean on the eggplant, long beans and bok choy for volume and fibre.

title: Beef Caldereta
description: Beef chunks braised low and slow in a tomato sauce with potatoes, carrots and bell peppers, enriched with liver spread until glossy and deep red — a special-occasion stew with Spanish roots.

ingredients.item: beef chuck or brisket, cut into 1.5-inch cubes
carrots, peeled and sliced into rounds

ingredients.note: or blended chicken liver as a substitute; adds body and colour
optional, for the classic briny bite

steps: Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a wide pot and pan-fry the potatoes and carrots until the edges lightly brown; remove and set aside.
In the same pot, heat the remaining oil and sear the beef in batches until browned on all sides; set aside with the vegetables.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pot until softened and fragrant.
Return the beef to the pot, add the tomato sauce, broth and bay leaves, and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer 60-75 minutes, stirring occasionally and topping up liquid if it runs low, until the beef is fork-tender.
Stir in the liver spread until fully dissolved into the sauce, then season with salt and pepper.
Add the browned potatoes, carrots, bell peppers and olives; simmer uncovered 8-10 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the sauce has thickened.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Searing the beef and pan-frying the potatoes separately first, rather than dumping everything in together, is what gives caldereta its depth.
Liver spread is the traditional thickener — don't skip it for cheese, which makes a different (and sweeter) dish.
Like most braises, caldereta reheats and often tastes better the next day.
nutritionNote: A protein-rich, moderately fatty braise; the potatoes and carrots already supply starch and vitamin A, so keep the rice portion normal-sized rather than adding extra sides that pile on more carbohydrate.

title: Pineapple Chicken
description: Chicken braised with pineapple chunks and juice, carrots and bell pepper in a lightly creamy sauce — a sweet, kid-favourite spin on the everyday chicken stew.

ingredients.note: 20 oz / 567 g can; separate the chunks from the juice

steps: Marinate the chicken pieces in the reserved pineapple juice for 20-30 minutes.
Lift the chicken out, reserving the marinade, and pat it dry.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium-high heat and sear the chicken until lightly browned on both sides; set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the onion and garlic until softened, then return the chicken to the pot.
Pour in the reserved pineapple marinade and enough water to nearly cover the chicken; bring to a boil, then lower the heat, cover, and simmer 20-25 minutes until the chicken is cooked through.
Add the pineapple chunks and carrot; simmer 5 minutes until the carrot is just tender.
Stir in the evaporated milk and fish sauce, and simmer uncovered 3-4 minutes until the sauce lightly thickens.
Add the bell pepper, season with pepper to taste, and cook 2 minutes more until just tender; serve hot with rice.
tips: Use the canned pineapple juice as the marinade rather than discarding it — it tenderizes the chicken and seasons the sauce at the same time.
Add the bell pepper last so it keeps some crunch instead of going limp.
nutritionNote: A milder, lower-sodium chicken dish thanks to the fruit sweetness carrying much of the flavour; balance the natural sugar from the pineapple with a smaller rice portion and a side of leafy greens.

title: Chicken Inasal
description: Chicken legs marinated in vinegar, calamansi, lemongrass and ginger, basted with golden annatto oil while grilling — the smoky, tangy specialty of Bacolod, sold at every roadside inasalan.

ingredients.item: chicken leg quarters, scored ¼-inch deep
lemongrass, white part only, pounded and chopped

ingredients.note: steeped in the oil to colour it orange; or use 1 tsp annatto powder

steps: Combine the vinegar, calamansi juice, lemongrass, garlic, ginger, sugar and salt in a bowl.
Add the scored chicken, massage the marinade in well, cover and refrigerate 4-24 hours.
Warm the oil over low heat with the annatto seeds for 3-4 minutes until the oil turns deep orange, then strain out the seeds and stir in the melted butter to make the basting sauce.
Prepare a hot charcoal or gas grill and lightly oil the grates.
Lift the chicken from the marinade, letting excess drip off, and grill skin-side down 5-6 minutes until well marked.
Flip and continue grilling, basting regularly with the annatto oil, another 8-10 minutes until fully cooked and lightly charred.
Rest the chicken 3-4 minutes before serving.
Serve hot with garlic rice and a small dish of soy-calamansi dipping sauce.
tips: Scoring the chicken lets the marinade penetrate faster and helps it cook more evenly on the grill.
The overnight marinate is unattended time — do it the night before for a quick weeknight grill session.
No charcoal grill? A hot oven broiler or stovetop grill pan works, though you'll miss the smoke flavour.
nutritionNote: Grilled rather than fried, so it's leaner than most Filipino chicken dishes; pair with a vegetable side rather than extra oil-basted rice to keep the meal balanced.

title: Bicol Express
description: Pork belly simmered in coconut milk with shrimp paste and green chilies until the sauce turns thick and red-orange — the fiery Bicolano dish named after the train that once carried its heat to Manila.

ingredients.note: reduce to 3-4 for a milder pot
optional, for real heat — omit entirely for a family pot

steps: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and sauté the onion and garlic until softened.
Add the pork and cook, stirring occasionally, 5-7 minutes until lightly browned.
Stir in the shrimp paste and cook 1-2 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in the coconut milk, bring to a gentle simmer, and cook uncovered 15-18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pork is tender and the sauce reduces.
Stir in the coconut cream and the green finger chilies; simmer 5 minutes more.
Add the long beans and cook 3-4 minutes until just tender.
Stir in the Thai chilies if using, season with pepper, and simmer 2 minutes more.
Serve hot with plenty of steamed rice.
tips: Slice the chilies rather than leaving them whole if you want the dish properly spicy — whole chilies add only aroma.
The dish thickens as it cools, so loosen leftovers with a splash of coconut milk when reheating.
Balance the shrimp paste's saltiness by tasting before adding extra fish sauce or salt.
kidNote: Set aside a plain, mild portion of pork and coconut sauce for the kids before adding any sliced chilies — use only whole, uncut long green chilies in their pot for aroma, and keep the Thai chilies strictly for the adult pot.
nutritionNote: High in saturated fat from both pork belly and coconut milk, so serve smaller portions of sauce over rice, add a plain vegetable side, and avoid pairing it with another coconut-milk dish in the same week.

title: Laing
description: Dried taro leaves simmered low and slow in coconut milk with pork, shrimp paste and chili until the leaves turn silky and deep green — a Bicolano classic that rewards patience and a heavy hand off the spoon.

ingredients.note: sold pre-dried in Filipino grocers; do not substitute fresh raw taro leaves, which are toxic uncooked

steps: Combine the coconut milk, pork, onion, garlic, ginger and shrimp paste in a wide pot and bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat.
Simmer uncovered 8-10 minutes until the pork is nearly cooked through.
Lay the dried taro leaves on top of the liquid in an even layer without stirring.
Let the pot simmer undisturbed 20-25 minutes, occasionally pressing the leaves down gently with a spoon so they submerge, until they soften, darken and absorb most of the liquid.
Once the leaves have sunk and softened, gently fold them into the sauce without vigorous stirring, which can turn the dish bitter.
Stir in the coconut cream and chilies, and simmer 5 minutes more until the sauce thickens and clings to the leaves.
Season with pepper to taste, then remove from the heat.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Resist stirring while the leaves cook in the first 20 minutes — disturbing them too early is the most common cause of a bitter, itchy-tasting laing.
Fully dried, packaged taro leaves are both safer and far less likely to cause the throat-itch some fresh leaves can if undercooked.
Leftover laing tastes even better the next day once the coconut oil separates slightly and the flavour deepens.
kidNote: Taro leaves have a naturally earthy, slightly bitter edge that many kids resist — spoon a portion of sauce and leaves without any chili for the kids, mix it well into their rice, and offer it as a side rather than the main event the first few times.
nutritionNote: Taro leaves bring iron, calcium and fibre despite the rich coconut sauce; serve smaller portions given the saturated fat content and pair with a plain protein like grilled fish rather than another coconut-based dish.

title: Eggplant Omelet
description: Whole eggplants charred until smoky, peeled and flattened, then dipped in beaten egg and pan-fried until golden and fluffy — the everyday breakfast omelet Filipino households make with whatever eggplant is on hand.
steps: Grill the whole eggplants directly over an open flame or under a broiler, turning often, 8-10 minutes until the skin is fully charred and blackened and the flesh feels soft.
Let the eggplants cool slightly, then peel off the charred skin under running water, keeping the stem intact.
Flatten each eggplant gently with a fork, leaving the stem attached as a handle.
Season the beaten eggs with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat.
Holding each eggplant by the stem, dip it into the beaten egg, coating both sides well, then lay it in the hot pan.
Spoon a little extra egg over the top of each eggplant, and fry 2-3 minutes per side until golden and set.
Drain briefly on paper towels and serve warm with rice, sliced tomato and a dip of soy sauce and calamansi.
tips: Charring the eggplant directly over a flame, not just steaming it, is what gives tortang talong its smoky background flavour.
Keep the stem on while flattening and dipping — it's your handle and helps the omelet hold together.
Work in one pan at a time; adding too much egg-coated eggplant at once cools the oil and makes the coating stick.
nutritionNote: A quick, protein-and-fibre-friendly vegetable dish; pair with a lean grilled or fried side and a fruit serving, since the eggplant and egg alone are light on the plate.

title: Pork Menudo
description: Pork and liver simmered in a tomato sauce with potatoes, carrots, garbanzo beans and raisins — a hearty stew with a faint sweetness that shows up at Filipino gatherings and Sunday lunches alike.

ingredients.item: pork shoulder, cut into small cubes
pork liver, cut into small cubes
ingredients.note: or omit and add extra pork shoulder for a milder version

steps: Combine the pork with the soy sauce and calamansi juice; marinate 10-15 minutes.
Heat the oil in a pot and pan-fry the potatoes and carrots until lightly browned at the edges; remove and set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the onion and garlic until softened, then add the marinated pork and cook until browned.
Add the tomatoes and cook, mashing them into the pork, until they break down into a sauce.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then lower the heat, cover, and simmer 25-30 minutes until the pork is tender.
Stir in the liver and cook 3-4 minutes, just until it loses its raw colour.
Add the fried potatoes and carrots, garbanzo beans and raisins; simmer 8-10 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Stir in the bell pepper and fish sauce, season with salt and pepper, and cook 2-3 minutes more before serving hot with rice.
tips: Adding the liver later, rather than browning it with the pork, keeps it from turning grainy.
Pan-frying the potatoes and carrots first helps them hold their shape through the simmer instead of turning mushy.
Menudo freezes and reheats well, making it a good make-ahead dish for a crowd.
nutritionNote: A balanced one-pot meal with protein, iron-rich liver and vegetables built in; the raisins add natural sugar, so a normal rice portion without extra sweet sides keeps the meal in balance.

title: Sweet and Sour Fish
description: Fried whole fish drenched in a glossy sweet-and-sour sauce with bell peppers, carrots and ginger — a bright, tangy way to turn an everyday market fish into a dinner-table centerpiece.

ingredients.item: whole tilapia or lapu-lapu, cleaned and scored
ingredients.note: or use firm fillets cut into large pieces

ingredients.item: red bell pepper, sliced into strips

steps: Season the fish with salt inside and out, then dredge lightly in cornstarch, shaking off the excess.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and fry the fish 4-5 minutes per side until golden and crisp; drain on paper towels.
Pour off most of the oil, leaving about 1 tablespoon, and sauté the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the carrot and cook 1-2 minutes, then add the bell pepper and stir-fry until just tender-crisp.
Pour in the vinegar, sugar, water and soy sauce; bring to a boil and let it bubble 1-2 minutes without stirring.
Stir the cornstarch slurry into the sauce and cook, stirring, until it thickens into a glossy glaze.
Place the fried fish on a serving platter and pour the hot sweet-sour sauce and vegetables over the top.
Serve immediately while the fish is still crisp, with steamed rice.
tips: Fry the fish until genuinely crisp — the hot sauce will soften it slightly, so it needs a head start.
Boil the vinegar briefly before thickening the sauce to cook off its raw sharpness.
Pour the sauce over just before serving so the fish doesn't sit and go soggy.
kidNote: Check the fried fish carefully for small bones before serving to the 6-year-old, or serve deboned fillets instead of the whole fish for the kids' plates.
nutritionNote: A lean protein dish once you account for the light frying; the carrot and bell pepper add vitamin A and C, and the sauce's sugar is balanced out by a normal, not oversized, rice portion.

title: Pancit Palabok
description: Rice noodles smothered in a thick orange annatto-shrimp sauce and topped with crumbled pork, boiled egg, chicharon and scallions — a party noodle dish built in layers rather than tossed together.

ingredients.item: shrimp, peeled and deveined, shells reserved

ingredients.note: simmer the reserved shrimp shells in water 10 minutes, then strain; or use fish or chicken stock
or 3 tbsp oil steeped with 2 tbsp annatto seeds, strained
or extra crushed chicharon if unavailable

steps: Soak the rice noodles in room-temperature water 15-20 minutes until pliable, then drain.
Bring a pot of water to a boil and blanch the noodles 1-2 minutes until just tender; drain and divide among serving plates.
Heat the oil in a pan and sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant, then add the ground pork and cook until browned.
Add the shrimp and cook 1-2 minutes until pink; lift out half the shrimp and pork mixture to use as a topping later, leaving the rest in the pan.
Pour in the shrimp stock and annatto powder, stirring until the broth turns deep orange, then bring to a simmer.
Stir in the fish sauce, then slowly add the cornstarch slurry, stirring constantly, until the sauce thickens into a loose, clingy gravy; season with salt and pepper.
Ladle the hot sauce generously over the noodles on each plate.
Arrange the reserved pork-shrimp mixture, sliced egg, chicharon, tinapa flakes and green onions on top, and serve immediately with calamansi halves for squeezing.
tips: Add the cornstarch slurry gradually and stop as soon as the sauce coats the back of a spoon — it thickens further as it sits.
Keep the noodles, sauce and toppings separate until the table is ready; palabok goes gummy if it sits assembled too long.
Making your own shrimp stock from the shells is a small extra step that noticeably deepens the sauce's flavour.
nutritionNote: A carb-forward party dish with good protein from pork, shrimp and egg; go light on the chicharon topping and add a vegetable side or soup to round out the meal.
